The Pythagorean identity is

$$
\cos^2{\theta}+\sin^2{\theta}=1.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to simplify trigonometric expressions. For example, let's try to simplify the following:

$$
2\sin \theta \left(\sin \theta + \dfrac {\cos^2 \theta} {\sin \theta}\right)
$$

We first expand the parentheses, and then simplify the resulting expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}\theta (\operatorname{sin}\theta +\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }) & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }} \\  & =2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta  \\  & =2({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, as follows:

$$
2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta) =2\cdot 1 = 2
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
2\sin \theta \left(\sin \theta + \dfrac {\cos^2 \theta} {\sin \theta}\right) = 2.
$$

Suppose we are given two vectors 
$\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,$ shown below. How do we compute the vectors $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$  and  $-5\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the standard basis $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?$

![](images/25/254809cbc834b493759a6fa09222a2c90c5fbfc3280d22e82470e760a7a4c508.png)

To compute $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},$ we collect all of the $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s. We know that $\mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} & =({\color{red}2}\mathbf{i}+{\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j})+({\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i}+{\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =({\color{red}2}+({\color{red}-4}))\mathbf{i}+({\color{blue}3}+{\color{blue}4})\mathbf{j} \\  & ={\color{red}-2}\mathbf{i}+{\color{blue}7}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
$$
\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-2} \mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}7}\mathbf{j} =  \langle {\color{red}-2}, {\color{blue}7} \rangle = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 2} \\ {\color{blue}7}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To compute $-5\mathbf{a},$ we multiply each of the components by $-5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \mathbf{a} & =-5({\color{red}2}\mathbf{i}+{\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(-5\cdot {\color{red}2})\mathbf{i}+(-5\cdot {\color{blue}3})\mathbf{j} \\  & ={\color{red}-10}\mathbf{i}+{\color{blue}-15}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
$$
-5\mathbf{a} =  {\color{red}-10} \mathbf{i}+ {\color{blue}-15} \mathbf{j} = \langle {\color{red}-10}, {\color{blue}-15} \rangle = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 10} \\ {\color{blue}- 15}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{\color{red}2},{\color{blue}5}⟩+⟨{\color{red}-3},{\color{blue}7}⟩ &= ⟨{\color{red}2}+({\color{red}-3}),{\color{blue}5}+{\color{blue}7}⟩ \\ &= ⟨{\color{red}-1},{\color{blue}12}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{}\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}2} \\ {\color{blue}5}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}-3} \\ {\color{blue}7}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}2}+({\color{red}-3}) \\ {\color{blue}5}+{\color{blue}7}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}-1} \\ {\color{blue}12}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot ⟨{\color{red}2},{\color{blue}5}⟩ &= ⟨(-5)\cdot {\color{red}2},(-5)\cdot {\color{blue}5}⟩ \\ &= ⟨{\color{red}-10},{\color{blue}-25}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}2} \\ {\color{blue}5}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-5)\cdot {\color{red}2} \\ (-5)\cdot {\color{blue}5}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}-10} \\ {\color{blue}-25}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we have two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a} & ={a}_{1}\mathbf{i}+{a}_{2}\mathbf{j}+{a}_{3}\mathbf{k} \\ \mathbf{b} & ={b}_{1}\mathbf{i}+{b}_{2}\mathbf{j}+{b}_{3}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross product $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf b$ can be calculated using the following determinant:

$$
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = 
	\left|
		{\begin{array}{ccc}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{array}}
	\right|
$$

For instance, suppose that we have the two vectors $\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,-1,5 \rangle$, $\mathbf{b} = \langle -1,4,2 \rangle$. We can find the cross product of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 5 \\ -1 & 4 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 5 \\ 4 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 5 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot 2-5\cdot 4)\mathbf{i}-(2\cdot 2-5\cdot (-1))\mathbf{j}+(2\cdot 4-(-1)\cdot (-1))\mathbf{k} \\  & =-22\mathbf{i}-9\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-22,-9,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We have been using the following formula to compute the cross product of two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{2} & {b}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{1} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =({a}_{2}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{2})\mathbf{i}-({a}_{1}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{1})\mathbf{j}+({a}_{1}{b}_{2}-{a}_{2}{b}_{1})\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

But where does this formula come from? Let's find out.

Suppose we want to find the cross product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ for $\mathbf{a}=a_1\mathbf{i}+a_2\mathbf{j}+a_3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=b_1\mathbf{i}+b_2\mathbf{j}+b_3\mathbf{k}.$ Using properties of the cross product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =({a}_{1}\mathbf{i}+{a}_{2}\mathbf{j}+{a}_{3}\mathbf{k})\times ({b}_{1}\mathbf{i}+{b}_{2}\mathbf{j}+{b}_{3}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{1})\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{i}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{2})\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{j}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{3})\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{k} \\  & +({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{1})\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{i}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{2})\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{j}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{3})\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{k} \\  & +({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{1})\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{i}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{2})\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{j}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{3})\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the cross product of two parallel (collinear) vectors is equal to $\mathbf 0,$ we have

$$
\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{k} = \mathbf 0.
$$

Also, using the definition of the cross product we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{j}=\mathbf{k}, & \hspace{2em}\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{i}=-\mathbf{k}, \\ \mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}, & \hspace{2em}\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{j}=-\mathbf{i}, \\ \mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}, & \hspace{2em}\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{k}=-\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{1})\underbrace{\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{i}}_{=\mathbf{0}}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{2})\underbrace{\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{j}}_{=\mathbf{k}}+({a}_{1}\cdot {b}_{3})\underbrace{\mathbf{i}\times \mathbf{k}}_{=-\mathbf{j}} \\  & +({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{1})\underbrace{\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{i}}_{=-\mathbf{k}}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{2})\underbrace{\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{j}}_{=\mathbf{0}}+({a}_{2}\cdot {b}_{3})\underbrace{\mathbf{j}\times \mathbf{k}}_{=\mathbf{i}} \\  & +({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{1})\underbrace{\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{i}}_{=\mathbf{j}}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{2})\underbrace{\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{j}}_{=-\mathbf{i}}+({a}_{3}\cdot {b}_{3})\underbrace{\mathbf{k}\times \mathbf{k}}_{=\mathbf{0}} \\  & =({a}_{2}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{2})\mathbf{i}-({a}_{1}{b}_{3}-{a}_{3}{b}_{1})\mathbf{j}+({a}_{1}{b}_{2}-{a}_{2}{b}_{1})\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above is equal to the formula given for the cross product of two general vectors using the determinant.

Consider the function $f(x) = x^2.$ The **definite integral** **of** $\mathbf f(x)$ **between** $\mathbf{x=1}$ and $\mathbf{x=2}$ is denoted

$$
\int_1^2 x^2 \, \textrm d x.
$$

Geometrically, this definite integral can be interpreted as the **signed area** bounded between the curve $y=f(x),$ the lines $x=1$ and $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/fd/fdff7865deed3d5329495bac5dfe045fefca9c09c6fccb7cd02b73d40de8bf69.png)

The area is taken as positive (with a plus sign) if the corresponding region lies above the $x$-axis and as negative (with a minus sign) if the region lies below the $x$-axis. 

To calculate this area, we use a theorem known as the **fundamental theorem of calculus**, which states the following:

> *If $f(x)$ is a function that's continuous on an interval $[a,b]$, and there exists a function $F(x)$ such that $F'(x) = f(x)$ on $[a,b]$, then*

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm{d}x = F(b) - F(a).
$$

So how do we use this to calculate our definite integral $$
\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm{d}x?
$$ We just need to follow a few steps:

 **Step 1**: Find the *indefinite* integral (also known as the antiderivative) of the function using the power rule. We can ignore the constant of integration.

$$
\int x^2 \, \textrm d x = \dfrac{x^3}{3}
$$

 

**Step 2**: Write the lower and upper limit next to the result.

$$
\int_1^2 x^2 \, \textrm d x = \dfrac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_{\color{red}1}^{\color{blue}2}
$$

 

**Step 3**: Evaluate the antiderivative between the upper and lower limit, and subtract them.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x & =\frac{({\color{blue}2})^{3}}{3}-\frac{({\color{red}1})^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\int_1^2 f(x)\,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac73.
$$

To convert the parametric equations of a circle to a Cartesian equation, we can eliminate the parameter $\theta$ using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

To demonstrate, consider the circle defined parametrically as

$$
x=5\cos\theta,\quad y=5\sin\theta, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $x^2+y^2 = 25.$

The **scalar triple product** of three vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is defined as $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).$

For example, suppose we have three vectors $\mathbf{a} = \langle -1,2,1 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b} = \langle 1,1,-2 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c} = \langle 0,3,1 \rangle.$ Let's compute their scalar triple product, $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).$

First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 3)\mathbf{i}-(1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+(1\cdot 3-1\cdot 0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =7\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨7,-1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =⟨-1,2,1⟩\cdot ⟨7,-1,3⟩ \\  & =(-1)\cdot 7+2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 3 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** The scalar triple product takes its name from the fact that it multiplies three vectors together and always results in a scalar.

Later, we will learn some geometric intuition behind the scalar triple product. But for now, we will focus on computing the scalar triple product.

It turns out that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

That is to say, if $\mathbf{a} = \langle a_1,a_2,a_3 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b} = \langle b_1,b_2,b_3 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c} = \langle c_1,c_2,c_3 \rangle,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})=\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

A proof of this result will be given at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's focus on computing the scalar triple product using the determinant above.

The scalar triple product has two important properties.

First, scalars can be factored out of the product. For example,

$$
({\color{red}2}\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot ({\color{red}2}\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times {\color{red}2}\mathbf{c}) = {\color{red}2}\left[ \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\right].
$$

Second, if we swap exactly two vectors in the scalar triple product, the result changes sign. For example, swapping $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ we have

$$
{\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \cdot ( {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \times \mathbf{c}) = - {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \cdot ( {\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \times \mathbf{c}).
$$

Note that if we swap twice, then the result remains the same, because the negatives cancel out. For example, swapping $\color{red}\mathbf{a}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{b}$ and then swapping $\color{red}\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\color{red}\mathbf{a}}\cdot ({\color{blue}\mathbf{b}}\times \mathbf{c}) & =-{\color{blue}\mathbf{b}}\cdot ({\color{red}\mathbf{a}}\times \mathbf{c}) \\  & =-(-{\color{blue}\mathbf{b}}\cdot (\mathbf{c}\times {\color{red}\mathbf{a}})) \\  & ={\color{blue}\mathbf{b}}\cdot (\mathbf{c}\times {\color{red}\mathbf{a}}).\end{aligned}
$$

These properties arise naturally from the fact that the scalar triple product can be computed as a determinant.

1\. If we multiply a row of the matrix by a number, then the determinant is multiplied by that number:
  $$
{\left| \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{red}2} {a}_{1} & {\color{red}2} {a}_{2} & {\color{red}2} {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{array} \right|} = {\color{red}2} {\left| \begin{array}{ccc}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{array} \right|}
$$

2\. If we swap two rows, then the determinant changes sign:
  $$
{\left| \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{red}{a}_{1}} & {\color{red}{a}_{2}} & {\color{red}{a}_{3}} \\ {\color{blue}{b}_{1}} & {\color{blue}{b}_{2}} & {\color{blue}{b}_{3}} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{array} \right|} = -  {\left| \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}{b}_{1}} & {\color{blue}{b}_{2}} & {\color{blue}{b}_{3}} \\ {\color{red}{a}_{1}} & {\color{red}{a}_{2}} & {\color{red}{a}_{3}} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{array} \right|}
$$

We have been using the fact for three vectors $\mathbf{a} = \langle a_1,a_2,a_3 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b} = \langle b_1,b_2,b_3 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c} = \langle c_1,c_2,c_3 \rangle,$ the scalar triple product can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})=\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

But why is this true? To understand where this result comes from, first notice that in the formula for the triple product, the cross product can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when we take the dot product with $\mathbf{a},$ we get an expression that is just the cofactor expansion across the first row of the matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =({a}_{1}\mathbf{i}+{a}_{2}\mathbf{j}+{a}_{3}\mathbf{k})\cdot (\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2}\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k}) \\  & ={a}_{1}\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}-{a}_{2}\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}+{a}_{3}\begin{vmatrix}{b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {b}_{3} \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {c}_{3}\end{vmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Given a curve $C$ parametrized by a function $\mathbf{r}(t)$, we can approximate the arc length by breaking up the curve into many small line segments and adding up their lengths.

To do this, we first choose a finite number of points $P_0,$ $P_1,$ $\cdots,$ $P_n$ along $C$ and form the polygonal path

$$
\overline{P_0P_1} \cup \overline{P_1P_2} \cup \cdots \cup \overline{P_{n-1}P_n},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/2d/2d320e6a0f63a823e049203203cbc13c210e80bc98aab5a53bcb4e5299240920.png)

Then, we can approximate the arc length as the sum of the lengths of the line segments:

$$
L \approx \, \big\| \overline{P_0P_1} \big\| + \big\| \overline{P_1P_2} \big\| + \ldots + \big\| \overline{P_{n-1}P_n} \big\|.
$$

If $P_k$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t_k),$ then by the mean value theorem,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖\overset{―}{{P}_{k-1}{P}_{k}}‖ & =‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}({c}_{k})‖({t}_{k}-{t}_{k-1}) \\  & =‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}({c}_{k})‖\mathrm{Δ}{t}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

for some intermediate point $c_k \in [t_{k-1}, t_k],$ where $\Delta t_k = t_k - t_{k-1}.$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & \approx \hspace{0.167em}‖\overset{―}{{P}_{0}{P}_{1}}‖+‖\overset{―}{{P}_{1}{P}_{2}}‖+…+‖\overset{―}{{P}_{n-1}{P}_{n}}‖ \\  & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{n}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}({c}_{k})‖\mathrm{Δ}{t}_{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a Riemann sum, and the closer the points $P_k$ are to each other, the better our approximation will be. So, in the limit as $n\to\infty$ (or $\Delta t_k \to 0),$ we have

$$
L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}  \| \mathbf r'(c_k) \| \Delta t_k=\int_{a}^{b} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve $C$ given by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad    t \in [0,1].
$$

 

The length of this curve is given by

$$
L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

To compute $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|,$ we take the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ and compute its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\right),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}t⟩, \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{({t}^{2})^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the curve $C$ is given by the integral

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}|t|\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this integral using substitution. Let $u = t^2+1,$ then $\textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.$ Therefore, our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating double integrals by changing the variables to polar coordinates is often easier than using Cartesian coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\left( {x^2 + y^2} \right)\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is the disk with center $(0,0)$ and radius $2,$ shown below.

![](images/94/945f3881b5348fffb922d7b57fb42a6262eb03861fb5aa2411b947a16dcb3b59.png)

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to plane polar coordinates because

- the domain $D$ is a disc of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ which has a simple polar representation, and

- the integrand $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$ can also be expressed simply in polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf T,$ defined by

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \quad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/99/9901b20d218bef2935dba64612495874d08388dc6d7ae21f8a1de596296bc276.png)

             

To express our integral in terms of polar coordinates, we will use the **change of variables formula,** given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, {{\color{black}{\mathrm d A}}} = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  {{\color{black}{r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta}}}.
$$

When expressing our integral in polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{black}{\textrm d A}} = {\color{black}{r\,\textrm d r\textrm d \theta}}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of $r.$

Now, applying the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}{\color{black}\mathrm{d}A} & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})\hspace{0.222em}{\color{black}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta } \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot 4 \\  & =8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\left( {x^2 + y^2} \right)\,\mathrm d A}} = 8\pi.
$$

In terms of transformations, the change of variables formula maps the non-rectangular integration domain $D$ to the rectangular domain $\Delta,$ making the integral much easier to evaluate.

Let's get a little more practice at writing regions in polar coordinates.

Consider the semicircular disc of radius $1$ centered $(1,0)$ in the first quadrant, shown below. The equation of the curve is $y=\sqrt{2x-x^2}.$

![](images/0f/0f4aec039a0de31d8f5ea24dc9db8c83f236dfd66e9f181768dae45ab0fd6b07.png)

First, we recall that the following equations relate Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's now use the above formulas to write the function $y=\sqrt{2x-x^2}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2x-{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = 2\cos\theta.$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta.$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=2\cos\theta$ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](images/35/3584d2f0d9ee2c0ce469bfc117c67c1efd1f4fd08c96c7beef00198624977d06.png)

Secondly, $\theta$ can vary between $\theta=0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](images/2c/2c5731478941621db03e8949eac217dcdfc604b3efd0312b56c59b9874d6be98.png)

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2\cos\theta, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

We can evaluate triple integrals by changing the variables to cylindrical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the finite region enclosed between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2,$ as shown below.

![](images/a6/a63e349d2776fe07077379b9d603e32ad2ff264cfa8005a226422b44f7e100fe.png)

 

This is a challenging integral to evaluate as it currently stands. However, we should recognize that the problem naturally lends itself to cylindrical polar coordinates.

Recall that if $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/b2/b2f8a6fe7f21b062eec294522e411c1e471b564eae68763d4767f917d65b54b0.png)

Notice that the region $R$ is

- bounded below by $z = 0,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 1 - x^2 - y^2 = 1 - r^2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 1-r^2 \right\}.
$$

![](images/da/dae76df462a695e655ffdde01559d19bf245aa6d601100fb8c7bc1024106a4c8.png)

 

To express our integral in terms of cylindrical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula, given by

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, {\color{blue}\mathrm{d}V} = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

When expressing our integral in cylindrical polar coordinates, we must write 

$$
{\color{blue}{\textrm{d}V}} = {\color{blue}r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta}.
$$

It's important not to forget the extra factor of ${\color{blue}{r}}.$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})\cdot r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}{r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\cdot r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\bbox[white, 2pt]{{\color{black}1}}}{\int }_{0}^{\bbox[white, 2pt]{{\color{black}1-{r}^{2}}}}\bbox[white, 2pt]{{\color{black}{r}^{3}}}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black}1 - r^2 }} \bbox[2pt,white]{\color{black} r^3} \: \mathrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta
=
\dfrac{\pi}{6}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2 + y^2 \:\textrm{d}V = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.
$$

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P$ and $Q$ exist, then the **divergence** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F,$ is the scalar given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Notice that if we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as 

$$
\nabla =  \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} +  \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y},
$$

 

then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by the dot product

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F.
$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = 2xy\, \mathbf i + e^{yx} \, \mathbf j .
$$

Then, we can calculate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the dot product formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} \\  & =(\mathbf{i}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{∂}{∂x}+\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{∂}{∂y})\cdot (2xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{yx}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{yx}) \\  & =2y+x{e}^{yx}\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3,$ expressed in terms of its component functions as

$$\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$$

If the first partial derivatives of $P, Q,$ and $R$ all exist, then the **curl** of $\mathbf F,$ denoted $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F,$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^3$ given by

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \left(\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \right)\,\mathbf i + \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)\,\mathbf j + \left(\dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial y}\right)\,\mathbf k.$$

The formula above is pretty tough to remember. Luckily, there is an easier way. If we define the differential operator $\nabla$ (a.k.a. the "del" operator) as

$$\nabla = \mathbf i\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x} + \mathbf j\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial y} + \mathbf k\,\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}$$

then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is given by the cross product

$$\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F.$$

Expressing the quantity on the right-hand side as a determinant, we have

$$
\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \nabla \times\mathbf F = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

For example, suppose that the vector field $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=xz\,\mathbf{i}+ xy\,\mathbf{j}+yz\,\mathbf{k}.$$

Then we can calculate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ using the determinant formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ xz & xy & yz\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz)]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz)]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(z-0)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(0-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(y-0)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

For example, consider the region $D$ below.

![](images/6d/6d7573de141b9a640242644c64fc79a002d93b595fc0d05d1e9ad75317358cb3.png)

Suppose that $\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ defined over $D,$ and

$$
\oint\limits_{C_1}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = 12, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_2}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = -8, 
\qquad 
\oint\limits_{C_3}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = -2,
$$

where $C_1$ is oriented counterclockwise, and $C_2,$ and $C_3$ are oriented clockwise. Let's use this information to calculate the value of the circulation $\Gamma,$ given by

$$
\Gamma = \displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/ab/ab13029d8b9168b384e14d2ae5f10d63c80b3fc8ca46695f59c2405443fa6b14.png)

Since the value of each line integral is given for a positively oriented curve, we can calculate the total circulation over $D$ by summing the circulations over each boundary curve. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Γ} & ={∮}_{∂D}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & =12+(-8)+(-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

As a concrete example, let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C,$ parametrized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2\cos t, \: \sin t \rangle, \qquad t \in \left [0, 2\pi \right).
$$

The region $D$ and its positively oriented bounding curve $C$ are shown below.

![](images/a6/a6d9fe9cad4ccee56d5d61457c475b41371e0705f1aeccd3a18fb4a3fa8e127c.png)

To calculate the area of $D$ using Green's theorem, we need to find a vector field whose scalar curl equals unity everywhere on $D.$ So, let's choose

$$
P(x,y) = -y, \qquad Q(x,y) = 0.
$$

Indeed, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 0 - \left(-1\right) = 1. \qquad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}
$$

Therefore, since $C$ is a positively oriented path, the area of $D$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting our expressions for $P$ and $Q$ into the above, we get

$$
\oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}x + Q \: \text{d}y = -\oint\limits_C y \: \text{d}x.
$$

 

Let's now evaluate the integral using the usual methods. The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
\mathbf{r'}(t) = \langle -2\sin t, \: \cos t \rangle.
$$

So we can calculate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\left(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}2t}{2}\right)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={[t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\textrm{Area}(D)  =2\pi.
$$

When proving Green's theorem, we typically start by assuming that $D$ is a so-called **simple region** (that is, a region that is both type I and type II). Then, Green's theorem is *extended* to include regions that are not simple.

Let's suppose that we've proved that Green's theorem is true for type I and type II regions. How can we use this to show that Green's theorem is also true for regions containing holes?

To illustrate how this is done, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle\oint\limits_{\partial D} \mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$

 

where $D$ is the annular region below.

![](images/57/57c22c3d7a92ce4a1a1a798f7e6a861ded2e9a6be4d8d98c36869fe29e2783d0.png)

Note that $\partial D= C_1\cup C_2$ is positively oriented. 

Now, imagine splitting $D$ into two regions $D_1$ and $D_2$ by means of *cuts* along the segments $[-4, -2]$ and $[2,4]$ on the $x$-axis, as shown below 

![](images/e7/e7f0d41c3fb909073cdaf4ea23f4ab617032e0d24bdc8d9b9e3724e7d56abe3b.png)

Notice that $D_1$ and $D_2$ are positively oriented type I regions. In addition, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1} & ={C}_{3}\cup {C}_{8} \\ {C}_{2} & ={C}_{5}\cup {C}_{10} \\ ∂{D}_{1} & ={C}_{3}\cup {C}_{4}\cup {C}_{5}\cup {C}_{6}, \\ ∂{D}_{2} & ={C}_{8}\cup (-{C}_{6})\cup {C}_{10}\cup (-{C}_{4})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the circulation of $\mathbf F$ over $\partial D$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup \hspace{0.167em}{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{8}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{5}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{10}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & +\underbrace{{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{-{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{6}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{-{C}_{6}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}}_{0} \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{3}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{5}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{6}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & +{\int }_{{C}_{8}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{-{C}_{6}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{\int }_{{C}_{10}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{-{C}_{4}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={∮}_{∂{D}_{1}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}+{∮}_{∂{D}_{2}}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={∮}_{∂{D}_{1}}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x+Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y+{∮}_{∂{D}_{2}}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x+Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

 

To summarize,

$$
\oint \limits_{\partial D}\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r = \iint_\limits{D}\left(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is just Green's theorem for the region $D.$

To calculate the line integral of a function $f(x,y)$ along a curve $C,$ we use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ must be parametrized by the vector function $\mathbf r(t)$ to apply this formula.

Now suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} \dfrac{y}{x} \,\textrm ds,
$$

where $C$ is the section of the curve $y = x^2$ between the points $(0,0)$ and $(1,1).$

![](images/a8/a8a3fe6c05479258f84aa074398e92a8a849fa4d015feb450aeef6a6066a870e.png)

To reduce the calculation of the line integral to a parametric case, we must first parametrize the curve.

Notice that the curve $C$ is of the form $y = y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y = y(t) =  t^2.$ This gives the following parametrization for $C\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle t, t^2 \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 1.
$$

Computing $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{({x}^{'}(t))}^{2}+{({y}^{'}(t))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, using $x=t$ and $y=t^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) &=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{{t}^{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the line integral in terms of $t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\hspace{0.167em}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t\end{aligned}

Suppose we want to compute the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is a washer enclosed between two circles centered at $(0,0)$ with radii $1$ and $2,$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/47/4752982aaf806b9e3b9c4d28d7a92bd01c3ff6a68afcca4235061a01b2fbc86f.png)

The easiest way to solve this problem is to convert it to polar coordinates. Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/e0/e0cc6c7f92704365c3ce15b91d85f703330b767a01f1f773b014cf61620563a3.png)

             

The change of variables formula for polar coordinates states 

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )}\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 7 \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}} = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}.
$$

A vector field $\mathbf F$ is **conservative** if there exists a scalar function $f$ such that 

$$
\mathbf{F} = \nabla \! f.
$$

If such a function $f$ exists, it is called a **potential function** for $\mathbf F.$

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = 2x\,\mathbf i + 2y\,\mathbf j.
$$

The function $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$ is a potential function for $\mathbf F$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{F}.\end{aligned}
$$

Not all vector fields are conservative. However, conservative vector fields have many interesting and useful properties, as we'll soon discover.

Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}({r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

First, recall that if $C$ is parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then 

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},
$$

where it is assumed that $C$ is positively-oriented. 

Substituting our expression for $\mathbf n$ into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that $\textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot \left(\frac{{y}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{x}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}}{||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||}\right)||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot \left(\frac{{y}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{x}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}}{\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||}}\right)\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x(t),y(t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot ({y}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{x}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P(x(t),y(t)){y}^{'}(t)-Q(x(t),y(t)){x}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now derive a general formula for the flux through an *upward-oriented* Cartesian surface.

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S
=
\iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Consider a surface $S$ given by the equation $z=g(x,y).$ The canonical parameterization of the surface is

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle.
$$

Computing the tangent vectors to the grid curves, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'} & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{vmatrix}=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the $\mathbf k$-component is positive, which indicates that our surface is upward-oriented.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We summarize as follows:

- *For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We have analogous results for surfaces of the form $y = h(x,z)$ and $x=k(y,z){:}$

- *For a surface $S$ given by $y = h(x,z)$ for $(x,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} + Q - R\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf j$-component is positive.*

- *For a surface $S$ given $x = k(y,z)$ for $(y,z) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by*

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( P - Q\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial y} - R\dfrac{\partial k}{\partial z} \right) \textrm{d}A,
$$

*where the unit normal to the surface is chosen such that the $\mathbf i$-component is positive.*

A vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $\mathbf{F}.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(xy+1){e}^{xy}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{F}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
\mathbf{F}={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(xy+1){e}^{xy}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P=(x-a){e}^{x+y},\,Q=x{e}^{x+y}.
$$

 
Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=(x-a){e}^{x+y},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=(x+1){e}^{x+y}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a){e}^{x+y} & =(x+1){e}^{x+y} \\ (x-a){e}^{x+y}-(x+1){e}^{x+y} & =0 \\ (x-a-x-1){e}^{x+y} & =0 \\ -(a+1){e}^{x+y} & =0 \\ a & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=-1.$

Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=-1,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F}=2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2xyz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$

Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2xyz) \\  & =0+2xy+2xy \\  & =4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}4xy\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}4xy\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}2y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (4-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}t(-\operatorname{sin}t)+(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+\operatorname{sin}s\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}(st))(s\operatorname{cos}(st))+(\operatorname{sin}(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}(st)) \\  & =s{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(st)-s{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(st) \\  & =s({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(st)-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}(2st).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}2s)+\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s}\right)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s} \\  & =-2-2{\operatorname{cot}}^{2}2s \\  & =-2{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}2s.\end{aligned}
$$

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have

$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=0.$

{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}2u-4v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 0,\,-1\le v\le 5\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -4\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}4,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨z+x,\hspace{0.222em}y+2z,\hspace{0.222em}x-4y⟩{|}_{x=u,\hspace{0.167em}\,y=v,\hspace{0.167em}\,z=2u-4v} \\  & =⟨2u-4v+u,\hspace{0.222em}v+2(2u-4v),\hspace{0.222em}u-4v⟩ \\  & =⟨3u-4v,\hspace{0.222em}4u-7v,\hspace{0.222em}u-4v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨3u-4v,\hspace{0.222em}4u-7v,\hspace{0.222em}u-4v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\hspace{0.222em}4,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\  & =(3u-4v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-7v)\cdot 4+(u-4v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-6u+8v+16u-28v+u-4v \\  & =11u-24v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+x,\hspace{0.222em}y+2z,\hspace{0.222em}x-4y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(11u-24v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{5}{\color{blue}(11u-24v)}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}z+2x⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=y-2x$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$

For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x)=-2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}z+2x⟩{|}_{z=y-2x} \\  & =⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+(y-2x),\hspace{0.222em}y-2x+2x⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{y-x}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{y}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}z+2x⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (-2)-(y-x)\cdot (1)+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y-y+x+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y+x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+xy]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(1+x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={[x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+2-1-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $S$ is positively (outward) oriented, use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S.$

Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5y-3{z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2+5+0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid cylinder enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}3\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & =3{∭}_{R}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & =3\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =3\cdot \pi \cdot {3}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =54\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=\operatorname{sec}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1$ by ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} & =\frac{1}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\ {\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}\right)}^{2}+1 & ={\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}\right)}^{2} \\ {\operatorname{tan}}^{2}t+1 & ={\operatorname{sec}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{tan}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{sec}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{2}+1={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${y}^{2}={\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{2}+1.$
Find $\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{a}),$ if $2\mathbf{a}\cdot ((-3\mathbf{b})\times \mathbf{c})=10.$

First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\mathbf{a}\cdot ((-3\mathbf{b})\times \mathbf{c}) & =10 \\ 2\cdot (-3)\cdot [\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})] & =10 \\ \mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{a}) & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

$$

$$

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(2s\operatorname{sin}t)(\operatorname{sin}t)+(-4t\operatorname{sin}s)(t\operatorname{cos}s) \\  & =2s{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t-4{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}s\operatorname{cos}s \\  & =2s{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t-2{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}2s.\end{aligned}
$$
